faqs.question: Is there any real advantage to an IGCSE tutor who lives near Business Bay?
faqs.answer: Only one, and it is small: a tutor nearby can be at your tower sooner. Everything a parent actually wants from proximity, a specialist who knows the paper, who can start this week, and who can be verified, is unrelated to distance. Business Bay has no IGCSE school inside the district, so there is no local pool of teachers who happen to know your child's scheme of work. The binding constraint is whether somebody who has taught your child's exact syllabus code and tier has a free hour at the time you need. That is an availability question, and widening the search answers it.

faqs.question: We are moving from Business Bay to Downtown Dubai. Will the tutoring options change?
faqs.answer: No. The two districts are one canal crossing apart, neither has an IGCSE school inside it, both feed the same school clusters in Sobha Hartland, Al Safa and Al Quoz, and both face the same evening traffic. The local in-home tutor pool is effectively the same pool. Across the six central-corridor districts we compare on this page, the only variable that genuinely differs is what time a weeknight session can realistically start, which ranges from about 4pm in DIFC and Sobha Hartland to about 5pm in Meydan. Your postcode controls your start time and almost nothing else.

faqs.question: Sobha Hartland has two British schools inside it. Doesn't living there make tutoring easier?
faqs.answer: It makes the school run easier, which is not the same thing. Having a campus five minutes away does not produce a local tutor who has taught Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Chemistry 4CH1 at Higher tier and happens to be free on Wednesday at 5.30pm. Families living beside those campuses book online tuition for exactly the same reason Business Bay families do: the match they need is to a specific paper, and specific papers are not distributed by neighbourhood. The one real benefit is timing, since a five-minute commute means a 4pm session is achievable rather than theoretical.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child is entered for Core or Extended tier?
faqs.answer: Ask the school in writing, subject by subject, and ask what evidence the decision rests on. Most Dubai schools will answer within a few days and many already report it in a column parents do not read closely. This is worth doing immediately, because tier caps the grade that can be awarded: a Core-tier candidate cannot reach the higher grades regardless of effort, and if a sixth-form science course requires grade 6, the route closes. A Year 9 or early Year 10 student has time to change the decision. A Year 11 in the spring term usually does not.

faqs.question: Can a tutor get my child moved from Core to Extended tier?
faqs.answer: No, and anyone who says they can is overselling. The entry decision belongs to the school, made within the board's deadlines on the basis of internal assessment. What tutoring can do is change the evidence the school is looking at, which is why timing matters so much. If the concern is raised in Year 9 or early Year 10, a term of focused work on the harder topic strands can genuinely alter a borderline decision. If entries have already been submitted, the honest plan is to maximise the grade available within the tier and keep the sixth-form conversation realistic.

faqs.question: My child's report shows both number grades and letter grades. Which scale is which?
faqs.answer: Most Pearson Edexcel International GCSE specifications grade 9-1, and many Cambridge IGCSE specifications grade A*-G, so a child taking subjects from both boards in the same year receives both. The boards publish rough equivalences, but they are approximate rather than exact, and treating a grade 7 as an A can cause a sixth-form requirement to be misread. More usefully: the subject grade tells you very little about what to fix. Ask for component-level marks instead, because a weak practical paper and a weak theory paper need completely different work.

faqs.question: What does a weekly IGCSE tutor cost per month in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Taking monthly figures rather than hourly ones, Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table estimates roughly AED 240 to 600 a month for a weekly hour at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Published packages in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are other providers' published figures read in October 2026, not IB Gram prices. We point families to the free trial and the consultation instead of a published UAE rate card.

faqs.question: What exactly am I paying for when an in-home visit costs more?
faqs.answer: The travel. Bestimate puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, with independent home tutors reaching AED 200 to 500 once travel is priced in. The gap covers the drive to your tower in Business Bay, parking, the lift, and the polite twenty minutes at the end. It does not buy a more qualified teacher or a better match to your child's paper. Priced across two subjects over a school year, the travel premium is a substantial amount of money spent on logistics rather than on teaching.

faqs.question: Which exam series will my child in Dubai actually sit?
faqs.answer: The June series or the November series. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level examinations in a June series and a November series, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May/June and November each year. Important for UAE families: the Cambridge February/March series is offered to India only, so any plan built around a February or March exam window is built on the wrong country's calendar. Read the exact dates from the board's live timetable rather than from any tutoring website, including this one, because provisional timetables are revised before they become final.

faqs.question: What is an exam zone and why does our examinations officer keep mentioning it?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, and the timetable differs by zone. Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. Practically, that means your child's revision calendar must be built from the timetable your own school's examinations officer confirms, not from a version found online. It takes one email to confirm, and it is the cheapest piece of exam-season risk management available.

faqs.question: A tutoring site told us six IGCSE subjects are required for equivalency. Is that right?
faqs.answer: Five. Students on the British track must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and must also submit proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or above, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. This is worth knowing because at least one ranking tutoring site in this market publishes six, which is wrong. IB Gram does not perform or guarantee equivalency; verify the current requirement on moe.gov.ae or with your emirate's attestation authority before acting.

faqs.question: Does my child's IGCSE tutor need a permit, and how would I check?
faqs.answer: Yes. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and covers teachers in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published. Ask the tutor or provider directly about permit status; a reluctance to answer is itself informative.

faqs.question: Is hiring a teacher from my child's own Dubai school a sensible shortcut?
faqs.answer: It is a worse idea than it sounds. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Verify the exact current wording against ADEK's policy document, since this is press-reported. Beyond compliance, it collapses the useful separation between the person who teaches your child and the person who assesses them, and it removes the independent second opinion that is half of what tutoring buys.

faqs.question: Will a tutor help my child finish their coursework before the deadline?
faqs.answer: A tutor will teach the content, explain the assessment criteria, model the technique on a different example, and give feedback on your child's own draft. A tutor will not write the text, supply sentences to be copied, or edit the piece to completion. That boundary is not negotiable, because a malpractice finding falls on the student rather than on the tutor. There are providers in this market that sell completed assessed work; that offer is a reason to walk away from them. If a deadline is genuinely unreachable, the conversation to have is with the school, not with a tutor.

faqs.question: What if no tutor is free for my child's subject at the time we need?
faqs.answer: You will be told at the enquiry rather than matched to whoever is available. Mathematics, the three sciences, English, business, economics and computer science are reliably covered at both boards and both tiers. Narrower subjects and the 5pm to 7pm Gulf Standard Time peak are where gaps appear. Where no UAE-based specialist covers a paper, the match may be a specialist teaching into the Gulf timezone from elsewhere, stated before the trial. The hours that stay open longest for Business Bay families are 4.30pm and anything after 7.30pm.

faqs.question: Do you have an office or a centre in Business Bay we could visit?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram has no office, branch or tuition centre anywhere in the United Arab Emirates, and we do not send tutors to UAE homes; home visiting is a service we run only in India. All UAE tuition is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. We say this plainly because two things in this market are worth checking before you buy: whether a provider actually has the UAE premises its footer implies, and whether the phone number you are given is a UAE number. Both are easy to verify and both tell you something.

dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-business-ba.closingHeading: Start with the paper, not the postcode
dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-business-ba.closingBody: If you remember one thing from this page, make it this: find out which board, which syllabus code and which tier your child is entered for, and get the component-level marks from the school. Those four pieces of information are free, they take one email, and they are what makes a useful tutoring decision possible. Bring them to a short consultation on Gulf Standard Time and we will tell you which subjects justify tuition, which do not, and what the first four weeks would address. The trial lesson is free, no card is needed, and it ends with a diagnosis you can read. Business Bay, Downtown, DIFC or Meydan: the answer comes out the same, which is why we spent this page proving it rather than asserting it.

dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-city-walk.tutorsIntro: These tutors cover Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE subjects for students across City Walk, Al Wasl, Al Safa and the Jumeirah plots. Matching starts with the syllabus code on your child's timetable, because that is what determines which papers they will sit.

intro.heading: Four neighbourhoods, one answer: why proximity is the wrong variable
paragraphs: City Walk, Al Wasl, Jumeirah 1 and Al Safa sit within about four kilometres of each other on either side of Al Wasl Road. Parents in all four search the same phrase and get the same local-looking results, and in all four the local-looking answer runs into the same wall. The schools are close. The specialists are not evenly distributed, and a tutor is not a plumber.

Start with what is genuinely different between these streets. City Walk is low-rise apartments with a retail district attached, so households skew towards one or two children and towards evening availability. Al Wasl is villa stock along the main road, often with three children in three different year groups. Jumeirah 1 is older plots with a heavy British-curriculum primary intake. Al Safa holds Jumeirah College and Jumeirah Baccalaureate School within the same cluster, so one street can contain IGCSE, A Level and Diploma students at once. Those are real differences and they change the shape of a family's week.

What they do not change is the IGCSE problem. A Year 10 student at any of these addresses is sitting a named syllabus from Cambridge or Pearson, with a fixed paper structure, a fixed tier, and a published assessment objective breakdown. Whether the tutor lives eight minutes away or eight hundred kilometres away has no effect on whether they know that 0580 Paper 2 is the non-calculator Extended paper or whether they know the difference between 4MA1 Paper 1H and 2H. That knowledge is the product.

Proximity does have one measurable effect, and it is negative. A tutor willing to drive to City Walk for a 5pm start on a weekday is drawn from the set of people living close enough to make that work, which is a far smaller set than the people who teach the subject well. The narrower the requirement - Extended Additional Mathematics, Edexcel Further Pure, triple-award Physics for a student targeting an A* - the more the driving radius costs you. Families optimising for the postcode are quietly optimising against competence.

IB Gram resolves this by not pretending to offer the in-home product at all. Home visits are an India-only service; across the UAE every lesson is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. The rest of this page does the comparison work properly: the four neighbourhoods against each other, Cambridge against Edexcel, Core against Extended, the November window counted backwards, and the AED rates each provider in this market actually publishes.

One more framing point before the detail. An IGCSE course is two years long and almost every repairable problem inside it is cheaper to fix in Year 10 than in Year 11. Tier placement, board confusion, missing algebraic fluency and the habit of answering every question with everything known are all Year 10 problems that become Year 11 emergencies. A family who reads the next six sections in Year 10 is making a scheduling decision. A family reading them in April of Year 11 is triaging, and triage is expensive. That is the one genuine argument for acting on this search early rather than waiting for a report card to confirm what a marked paper would already have shown.

dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-city-walk.programmesIntro: An IGCSE student in City Walk is standing in the middle of a four-stage route. What the tutoring needs to do depends heavily on which stage they are at, because the assessment style changes sharply at 14 and again at 16.

programmes.name: Cambridge Lower Secondary
programmes.description: The three years before the IGCSE course starts, assessed internally with optional Checkpoint tests. Cambridge runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. This is the stage where algebraic fluency and scientific writing are either built or not, and the stage where a gap is cheapest to close.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools often set the Core or Extended tier decision in Year 9 or early Year 10 based on Lower Secondary performance. A City Walk family who wants Extended Mathematics kept open should be watching the Year 9 marks, not the Year 10 ones, because by then the set has usually been allocated.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses with numbered syllabuses: 0580 Mathematics, 0607 International Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry, 0610 Biology, 0653 Co-ordinated Sciences. Most subjects split into Core and Extended tiers with different papers and different grade ranges. Grades run A* to G, with 9-1 used on some syllabuses.
programmes.countryNote: Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone and cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask your school's exams officer which zone it sits in rather than downloading a generic timetable.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: The other major board in Dubai, with its own codes: 4MA1 Mathematics, 4PH1 Physics, 4CH1 Chemistry, 4BI1 Biology. Papers, tiering and question style differ from Cambridge, and some specifications are modular where Cambridge is linear. Grades are reported 9-1.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams are available in May/June and November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so always open the live official timetable.

programmes.name: A Level or IB Diploma
programmes.description: The IGCSE grade is the entry ticket. A Level sixth forms in Dubai typically set subject-specific grade requirements, and Diploma schools usually want evidence of performance in the relevant discipline before admitting a student to a Higher Level course. The Year 11 result therefore closes or keeps open the post-16 options.
programmes.countryNote: Around City Walk this matters because the British-curriculum schools nearest the area and the Diploma schools further out want different things. A student aiming at Higher Level sciences needs Extended-tier evidence; a student aiming at A Level Mathematics usually needs a specified grade in 0580 or 4MA1 rather than 0607.

dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-city-walk.subjectsIntro: These are the IGCSE subjects requested most often from this part of Dubai, named with the syllabus codes a tutor needs before the first lesson. Confirm the code on your child's own timetable: schools do change boards between cohorts.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
subjects.description: Extended sits Paper 2 without a calculator and Paper 4 with one. The Core tier sits Papers 1 and 3. Marks are lost to unsimplified surds, to premature rounding carried through a multi-step answer, and to method marks forfeited because no working was shown on a calculator paper.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Both Higher papers, 1H and 2H, permit a calculator, which shifts the difficulty towards multi-step problem solving and interpretation. Students arriving from a Cambridge set often under-practise the longer worded questions that carry five and six marks here.

subjects.name: International Mathematics (Cambridge 0607)
subjects.description: Designed to feed the IB, with a graphics calculator required and an investigation paper on some routes. It is not interchangeable with 0580 for A Level Mathematics entry, which is the detail families most often discover too late.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625 / Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Electricity and electromagnetism generate most of the requests and most of the lost marks. Students treat circuit questions as recall when they are reasoning problems, and lose the practical-skills marks by never having drawn a results table under time.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620 / Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles calculations, electrolysis and organic reaction pathways are the recurring weak points. The paper rewards precise language: a student who writes that a substance dissolves when the mark scheme wants dissociates has understood the chemistry and lost the mark anyway.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610 / Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.description: Content-heavy and deceptively easy to revise badly. The marks sit in applying knowledge to unfamiliar organisms and in data interpretation, not in recall. Transport in plants and homeostasis are the two topics most commonly abandoned mid-revision.

subjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0653)
subjects.description: Three sciences compressed into the equivalent of two subjects, which suits a student who needs breadth without three separate specifications. It closes some post-16 doors, so check the sixth-form entry requirement before choosing it in Year 9.

subjects.name: English Language (Cambridge 0500 / 0990)
subjects.description: Directed writing and the composition task carry the heaviest marks. Students lose them by writing in the wrong register for the stated audience and by leaving no time for the second task, which is a pacing failure rather than a writing one.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 / 0511)
subjects.description: A different qualification from first-language English with different post-16 recognition. Families moving from another system should check which one the school has entered their child for, because the two are frequently confused in Dubai admissions conversations.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Both reward structured evaluation. The commonest loss is a candidate who lists advantages and disadvantages and then stops, when the command term asked for a recommendation with justification. That is a technique fix, and a fast one.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
subjects.description: Taken alongside 0580 by strong mathematicians, and thinly staffed in most schools. It is the clearest example on this list of a subject where the tutor pool within a twenty-minute drive of City Walk is effectively empty.

subjects.name: Arabic and Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required in every Dubai private school alongside the international curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and requires teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education to hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects.

regions.name: City Walk
regions.note: Apartment blocks off Al Safa Street with retail attached. Smaller households, fewer simultaneous year groups, and strong demand for single-subject evening slots rather than afternoon ones.

regions.name: Al Wasl
regions.note: Villa stock along Al Wasl Road directly inland of City Walk. Multi-child households are common, so a family here is often booking a Year 7 and a Year 11 on the same evening in different subjects.

regions.name: Jumeirah 1
regions.note: Older plots between the beach road and Al Wasl Road, heavily British-curriculum at primary. Students frequently stay in the same school through Year 11, so board continuity is high and board confusion is low.

regions.name: Al Safa
regions.note: Holds Jumeirah College and Jumeirah Baccalaureate School in one cluster. The practical consequence is mixed-curriculum streets, where neighbours are sitting IGCSE, A Level and the Diploma simultaneously.

regions.name: Jumeirah 2 and 3
regions.note: Further along the coast, with siblings often split between two schools in opposite directions. Afternoon slots are unreliable here; the first workable window is usually after 6pm.

regions.name: La Mer and Pearl Jumeira
regions.note: Newer waterfront stock immediately north. Younger intake overall, so demand concentrates on Year 7 to Year 9 preparation rather than on Year 11 examination technique.

regions.name: Umm Suqeim
regions.note: The stretch towards Al Sufouh, with longer school runs and a higher proportion of students already spending an hour a day in a car before any tutoring is added to the week.

regions.name: Al Manara and Al Safa 2
regions.note: Inland villa communities with concentrated demand for Extended Mathematics and triple-award science, driven by the sixth-form entry requirements at the nearby British-curriculum schools.

schoolClusters.note: The second ring, reached along Al Wasl Road or Sheikh Zayed Road. Several of these schools set specific IGCSE grade requirements for their own sixth forms, which is what makes the Year 11 result consequential.

sections.heading: What this search returns, and what it leaves out
paragraphs: An IGCSE tutor near me in City Walk is a local-intent query, so the results are filled with providers asserting local coverage. Very few of them tell you the thing that decides whether an hour of tutoring is useful: which board and which tier your child is entered for. That single fact changes the papers, the question style, the tiering and the grade range, and it is printed on the school's own entry confirmation.

Here is what the search leaves out in practice. Three of six researched competitor pages in this market publish no price at all, and the two that do quote US dollars rather than dirhams. Five of six carry no comparison table. None names a Cambridge administrative zone, and none counts an exam session backwards to an entry deadline. Those are not minor omissions. They are the four questions a parent asks within ten minutes of starting to look.

This page is organised to answer them in order, starting with the comparison the query implies and then moving to the board, the tier, the calendar and the cost. The neighbourhood comparison comes first because it is the premise of the search, and because once it is tested properly the rest of the decision becomes much simpler.

One thing to settle immediately. IB Gram does not run home visits in the UAE, so nothing in this comparison is written to make the in-home option look worse than it is. In-home tutoring is a real product with real advantages, sold by other providers at published rates reproduced further down. The argument here is only that for a named IGCSE syllabus, the specialist matters more than the street.

sections.heading: City Walk, Al Wasl, Jumeirah 1 and Al Safa compared
paragraphs: Take the four neighbourhoods and score them on the variables that actually govern a tutoring arrangement: how many schools are within a short drive, how many of those run IGCSE, how late a travelling tutor could realistically start on a weekday, and how deep the local specialist pool is for a narrow subject. The results are close enough to be interesting.

All four are well served for schools. All four have a workable evening window, though it shifts later as you move along the coast. Where they separate is household shape: City Walk's apartment stock produces single-subject bookings, Al Wasl's villas produce multi-child bookings, Jumeirah 1's stability produces fewer board changes mid-course, and Al Safa's mixed-curriculum streets produce the most confusion about which qualification a child is actually sitting.

None of that changes the specialist arithmetic. For Additional Mathematics 0606, Edexcel Further Pure, or triple-award Physics aimed at an A*, the pool reachable by car within twenty minutes of any of these four addresses is thin in exactly the same way. The comparison converges on a single answer, which is the point of running it: the answer is the same either way, and it is not the postcode.

There is one further variable worth naming, because parents rarely raise it and it decides more than traffic does. Demand along this strip is concentrated in the same months and the same two hours of the day. Every family in Al Safa and Al Wasl wants a slot between five and seven in the eight weeks before mocks, and a travelling tutor can physically serve two or three of them in an evening. That constraint is invisible in October and absolute in February, which is when the families who waited discover that the well-regarded local tutor they were told about has no capacity left at any price.
The table puts the four side by side. Read the last column, which is the one that survives after the convenience factors cancel out.

sections.heading: Cambridge or Edexcel: check before you buy an hour
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE are separate qualifications from separate awarding organisations. They cover similar ground and they do not examine it the same way. A tutor who prepares a student for the wrong one is not slightly off; they are teaching a different paper structure, a different tiering system and a different house style of question.

The practical differences are concrete. Cambridge 0580 Extended sits a non-calculator Paper 2 and a calculator Paper 4. Pearson 4MA1 Higher permits a calculator on both papers, which pushes the difficulty towards extended multi-step problems. Cambridge grades many syllabuses A* to G with 9-1 on others; Pearson reports 9-1. Some Pearson specifications are modular where the Cambridge equivalent is linear. Cambridge also allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version.

That zone point is worth repeating because it has a consequence. Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. A family who downloads a timetable from a search result rather than from the school's exams officer has introduced a real risk for no benefit.

Ask the school three questions and the matching problem mostly solves itself: which board, which syllabus code, and which tier. Those three answers go at the top of a tutoring enquiry. Everything after that is scheduling.

sections.heading: Core or Extended, and the ceiling set in Year 10
paragraphs: The tier decision is the most consequential academic choice an IGCSE student makes, and it is usually made by a school in Year 9 or early Year 10 based on Lower Secondary performance. Core and Extended sit different papers and carry different grade ranges. A student on the Core tier cannot reach the top grades however well they perform, because those grades are not available on that paper.

Parents in City Walk discover this at two moments. The first is when a Year 10 report shows a strong percentage against a capped grade and the numbers do not seem to agree. The second is when a sixth-form application names a grade the Core tier cannot produce. Both are avoidable with a conversation in Year 9, and both are expensive to fix in Year 11, when moving tier means catching up content the Extended set covered a year earlier.

The honest tutoring position is that a tier move is sometimes right and often not. A student placed on Core because of weak algebra can frequently be moved if the algebra is repaired early enough; a student placed there because they are working at the ceiling of their current confidence may do better with a strong Core grade than a weak Extended one. The question is which of those two situations you are in, and that is answerable from a marked paper rather than from an opinion.

Where a move is the right call, the work is specific and sequenced: the Extended-only content first, then the question styles the Core papers never asked for, then timed papers at the Extended tariff. A tutor who agrees to the move without auditing the gap is setting a student up to sit a harder paper with the same preparation.

sections.heading: The November series counted backwards
paragraphs: Nobody competing for this search publishes an exam calendar. That is odd, because the calendar is the thing that makes tutoring urgent or not, and the deadlines sit much earlier than parents expect. Entries close months before papers are sat, and results arrive months afterwards.

Take the UAE-correct example. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams run in May/June and November each year. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so the live official timetable is what a family should open rather than a date restated on a tutoring page.

For Cambridge, UAE candidates sit the June series with November as the resit route. The February and March series is offered to India only and does not apply here, which is a detail some tutoring content gets wrong with real consequences. Cambridge also runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October, which is a separate matter from IGCSE entries.

Counted backwards, a November resit means the decision is made in the summer, the entry is confirmed through the school in the autumn, and the useful tutoring block runs across September and October. A family who starts looking for a tutor in late October has bought the last three weeks of a twelve-week problem.

sections.heading: What the Jumeirah-strip market charges, cheapest first
paragraphs: Work up from the bottom of the market rather than down from the top, because the bottom is where most families start looking. Budget online tutoring, generally delivered by university students, is advertised from roughly AED 33-150 an hour: Tutopiya lists from AED 33-52 and EdFlik from AED 45-65. At that rate the person teaching is usually a year or two out of the syllabus themselves, which is fine for homework supervision and poor for examination technique.

The next step up is a qualified subject tutor working online, roughly AED 150-300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. This is the band most IGCSE requests from City Walk actually belong in. Above it, IB and IGCSE specialists run AED 200-450 or more, with TutorChase publishing AED 270 and Bestimate reporting AED 200-450 or above, and premium named tutors reach AED 500-650, with BartyED at AED 650.

The in-home column sits across the middle of that range at roughly AED 180-500 an hour including travel, with Bestimate reporting AED 180-350 and independent home tutors asking AED 200-500. Monthly packaging in the market runs around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599-1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour arrangement are AED 240-600 budget, AED 600-1,200 mid-range and AED 1,000-2,000 or more for specialist exam-year work.

Every figure in this section was published by somebody else and is reproduced so a parent can check it. None of it is an IB Gram price. IB Gram quotes after the free trial lesson, against a named tutor, a syllabus and a session length, and the trial is taken before any payment or card detail is involved.

sections.heading: What the travel premium actually buys
paragraphs: Set the two options against each other honestly. The gap between an online qualified tutor at the AED 150-300 band and an in-home visit at AED 180-500 is not a quality gap. It is the cost of a car, fuel and the hour of a working evening that the drive between Al Barsha and Al Safa Street consumes. That hour is real, the tutor is right to charge for it, and the family is right to ask what it delivers.

What it delivers is physical presence, and that has genuine value in some situations. A Year 7 student who cannot yet self-manage a session works better with an adult in the room. A household with unreliable connectivity has a problem online that disappears in person. A parent who wants to overhear the lesson gets that without asking.

What it costs is pool size and reliability. The tutor must live close enough to make the journey viable, which is a selection criterion unrelated to teaching quality, and the journey is the most common reason a session starts late or is cancelled. For Additional Mathematics, Further Pure or a specific board's practical paper, the set of qualified people who will also make that drive on a Tuesday can be empty.

IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE, so the comparison here is not a sales device. It is the reason the service is shaped the way it is. For a named IGCSE syllabus with a named weak paper, the family that optimises for the specialist gets a better result than the family that optimises for the postcode, and online delivery is what makes the first option available from City Walk at all.

sections.heading: Five subjects, not six: the equivalency rule to get right
paragraphs: Ministry of Education equivalency decides whether an IGCSE and post-16 profile is recognised for university entry inside the UAE, and one page currently ranking for these queries publishes the wrong subject count. The sourced rule for the British track is that a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade.

Two details follow from that and both matter in Dubai. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, which changes the arithmetic for a student who was counting them. And the threshold is a floor for recognition, not a target: a grade E meets equivalency and will not satisfy a competitive university programme, so the two conversations should not be confused with each other.

On the American track the same source sets English proficiency at IELTS academic 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, with mathematics requiring at least 450 in SAT Math before applying. The article read for this page does not mention EmSAT and states no IB points threshold, which is why no IB figure appears here. Verify the IB route on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate attestation authority directly before relying on any number you find online.

IB Gram describes this process and does not perform, submit, expedite or guarantee any part of it, and nothing about tutoring is required for equivalency. The reason it appears on a tutoring page is practical: a family who learns the five-subject rule in Year 10 chooses subjects differently from a family who learns it in Year 13.

process.title: Send the board, the code and the tier
process.description: Three facts from the school's entry confirmation: Cambridge or Pearson, the syllabus number, and Core or Extended. With those, a match can usually be proposed the same day. Without them, the first conversation is spent establishing which qualification your child is sitting, which is time nobody needs to spend.

process.title: A marked paper before a recommendation
process.description: A recent mock or past paper, marked against the published scheme, tells you where the marks went by topic and by assessment objective. That is the evidence a plan is built on. A recommendation made without it is a guess, however confidently it is delivered.

process.title: Free 45-minute trial with the named tutor
process.description: The first lesson is free, taken with the tutor who would teach the course, and no card details are collected beforehand. One trial per student per subject. The test afterwards is simple: did the tutor identify something specific that the school had not already said?

process.title: A plan with the school's dates on it
process.description: You get a short written plan listing the topics in order, the past papers to be sat, and the school's own mock and coursework dates. If a November series is in play, the plan runs backwards from the timetable window rather than forwards from the first lesson.

process.title: Marked work every week
process.description: Each session sets questions and the next one opens with them marked to the scheme, mark allocation visible. Parents receive the written feedback. The number reported is the mark on the paper, not an assessment of effort, because the mark is what the board will eventually award.

whyPoints.title: Board first, everything else second
whyPoints.description: Matching starts from the syllabus code because Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different examinations with different calculator rules and different paper structures. A tutor prepared for the wrong one is teaching a different course. Most enquiries arrive without this information, and establishing it is the fastest useful thing a provider can do.

whyPoints.title: The comparison is run honestly
whyPoints.description: This page compares four neighbourhoods and two delivery models and reports where the in-home option wins, because it does win for younger students and for households with connectivity problems. IB Gram does not sell home visits in the UAE, so there is nothing to gain from overstating the case against them.

whyPoints.title: A calendar nobody else publishes
whyPoints.description: Entry deadlines sit months before papers and results arrive months after. The sourced Pearson November 2026 window, the June results dates and the Cambridge June-and-November position for UAE candidates are all on this page, with the instruction to open the live official timetable rather than trust a restated date.

whyPoints.title: Prices with the publisher named
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here is attributed to the provider who published it and dated to when it was read. Three of six competitor pages in this market publish no price and two quote dollars. A family should be able to check a rate before speaking to anybody, and on this page they can.

whyPoints.title: Thin specialisms admitted, not hidden
whyPoints.description: Additional Mathematics, Further Pure and some practical papers have genuinely small tutor pools. Where nobody suitable is free, the answer given is that nobody is free, with an estimate of when that changes. Placing whoever is available and hoping costs a family a term and is the commonest failure in this market.

whyPoints.title: Nothing unverifiable on the page
whyPoints.description: No satisfaction percentages, no star ratings, no tutor headcounts, no average grades. Every statistic here is a cited regulator figure or a published market rate with its source named. That constraint removes the most common category of claim on competing pages, and it is deliberate.

faqs.question: Does an IGCSE tutor near me in City Walk mean someone who visits the apartment?
faqs.answer: Not through IB Gram. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time; home visits are an India-only service. Independent in-home tutors do work across City Walk and Al Wasl, and the Dubai market quotes them at roughly AED 180-500 an hour with travel included. The comparison worth making is pool size. A tutor who will drive to Al Safa Street for a 5.30pm start is selected partly for where they live, and that filter removes most of the people who specialise in a narrow syllabus such as Additional Mathematics or Edexcel Further Pure.

faqs.question: Is tutoring in Jumeirah 1 or Al Safa any different from City Walk?
faqs.answer: The households differ more than the tutoring does. City Walk's apartment stock tends to produce single-subject evening bookings. Al Wasl's villas produce multi-child bookings across different year groups. Jumeirah 1 students often stay in one school to Year 11, so board confusion is rare. Al Safa has two large schools in one cluster and therefore the most mixed-curriculum streets and the most uncertainty about which qualification a child is sitting. What does not differ is the specialist pool within a short drive, which is thin for narrow subjects at all four addresses.

faqs.question: How do I find out whether my child sits Cambridge or Edexcel?
faqs.answer: Ask the school's exams officer, or look at the entry confirmation that goes home before a series. The answer should include the board, the syllabus code and the tier, for example Cambridge 0580 Extended or Pearson 4MA1 Higher. This is the first thing a tutor needs. Cambridge Extended Mathematics includes a non-calculator paper and Pearson Higher does not, which changes what practice is useful. Guessing from a textbook cover is unreliable, because schools sometimes teach from one publisher's resources while entering candidates with a different board.

faqs.question: Are Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE equivalent for universities?
faqs.answer: Both are recognised international qualifications and universities treat them as comparable, so the choice is rarely a recognition problem. It is a preparation problem. The paper structures, tiering and question styles differ, so a student needs practice on their own board's papers rather than on whichever past papers are easiest to find online. Some Pearson specifications are modular where the Cambridge equivalent is linear. For UAE recognition, Ministry of Education equivalency counts five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education.

faqs.question: When do UAE students actually sit their IGCSE papers?
faqs.answer: Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level exams in a June series and a November series, and UAE candidates sit those two. The February and March series is offered to India only and should be ignored on a UAE timetable. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams run in May/June and November, with the November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026. Cambridge separately runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Always open the live official timetable through the school rather than relying on dates restated elsewhere.

faqs.question: What is the Cambridge zone problem I keep reading about?
faqs.answer: Every Cambridge centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and each zone has its own version of the timetable. Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. The practical consequence for a Dubai family is that a timetable downloaded from a search result may not be the one their school is working to. Ask the exams officer which zone the centre sits in, then use that version only.

faqs.question: Is a tier switch out of Core still realistic once Year 11 starts?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it needs an audit rather than an opinion. Core and Extended sit different papers and Core caps the grade available, so a move is the only route to the top grades. The cost is the Extended-only content the Core set never covered plus the longer, less scaffolded question styles. Whether that is recoverable depends on why the student was placed on Core. Weak algebra that can be repaired is a different situation from a student working at the ceiling of their confidence. A marked paper answers the question; a predicted grade does not.

faqs.question: How much does an IGCSE tutor cost around Jumeirah and Al Wasl?
faqs.answer: Working from the bottom of the market: budget online tutoring is advertised from roughly AED 33-150 an hour, with Tutopiya from AED 33-52 and EdFlik from AED 45-65. A qualified subject tutor online is roughly AED 150-300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150. Specialists run AED 200-450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180-500 including travel. Those are other providers' published rates as read in October 2026. IB Gram quotes after the free trial, against a named tutor, syllabus and session length.

faqs.question: Is the cheapest online tutoring a false economy for Year 11?
faqs.answer: Often, and for a specific reason. At the AED 33-65 band the person teaching is frequently a university student who sat the syllabus recently rather than someone who has marked it. That is adequate for homework supervision and for re-explaining content, and weak for examination technique, which is where most Year 11 marks are lost. If the problem is that your child does not understand moles, cheap help can work. If the problem is that they understand moles and score 4 out of 7 on the question, the gap is technique and it needs somebody who knows the mark scheme.

faqs.question: What happens in a lesson if nobody is in the room with my child?
faqs.answer: The student works rather than watches. A shared whiteboard they write on, screen sharing for past papers and mark schemes, and a recording available afterwards for revision before a timed paper. Questions are set between sessions and returned marked to the published scheme with the mark allocation shown, and parents get that written feedback. Sessions sit on Gulf Standard Time around the school day and move to post-Iftar slots during Ramadan on request. For a Year 7 or Year 8 student who cannot yet self-manage, an in-home arrangement is genuinely better, and this page says so.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects are hardest to find a local tutor for?
faqs.answer: Additional Mathematics 0606 is the clearest case: it is thinly staffed in schools and the pool within a twenty-minute drive of City Walk is effectively empty. Edexcel Further Pure is similar. After those come board-specific practical papers, where a tutor needs to know whether the school enters Paper 5 or Paper 6, and English as a Second Language at the Extended tier, which is frequently confused with first-language English. These are the subjects where online matching changes the answer from nobody suitable to somebody suitable.

faqs.question: Does my child still take Arabic and Islamic Education alongside IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Yes. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies in every Dubai private school regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies and states that combined classes are strictly prohibited. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education must hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects, and no different or additional content may be used without prior Ministry of Education permission.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does the Ministry count for equivalency?
faqs.answer: Five. The sourced rule requires a student to pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among the five, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. One page currently ranking for UAE tutoring queries states six, which is wrong. Treat grade E as a recognition floor rather than a target: competitive university programmes ask for far more than the equivalency minimum.

faqs.question: Do I have to tell the school we have hired a tutor?
faqs.answer: You are not obliged to, and it is usually the better choice. A subject teacher who knows a tutor is involved can say which topics to prioritise and share the mock breakdown, and that information makes the tutoring measurably more effective. It also removes any ambiguity if coursework is involved later. Keep a note of what each session covered. Visible, documented support is never the thing that creates a problem; undisclosed help with assessed work is, and that line matters more in some subjects than others.

faqs.question: What if we only need help for the last few weeks before the papers?
faqs.answer: That is a legitimate request and it should be shaped honestly. A short block can deliver examination technique, pacing, command-term discipline and timed-paper practice, and those gains are real and often visible in the next mock. What a short block cannot do is teach two years of content or repair a tier placement. The sensible version starts with a timed diagnostic paper marked to the scheme, then spends the remaining hours on the topics and assessment objectives where the marks actually went, with a fixed end date and no rolling commitment.

dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-city-walk.closingHeading: Start with three facts from the school
dubai/igcse-tutor-near-me-in-city-walk.closingBody: Board, syllabus code, tier. Send those three and a recent marked paper, and a specialist for that exact specification can usually be proposed within a working day or two. The first 45-minute lesson is free, taken with the named tutor over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with no card details collected beforehand. Afterwards you get a written plan with your school's mock and entry dates on it, and a quote against the named tutor and session length. intro.heading: The examination year has a calendar nobody shows you
paragraphs: Parents in Culture Village usually meet the IGCSE administrative calendar one item at a time and always slightly too late. The entry window has closed. The timetable turns out to differ from a friend's at another school. Results arrive on a date nobody had written down. A remark is possible but the deadline has nearly gone. Each of those is knowable months in advance, and each one changes what a tutor can usefully do.

Start with entries. The school's exam office makes them, within the board's window, months before the papers, and the entry fixes the board, the subject list and the tier. Everything a parent might want to influence about those three has to happen before that point. A conversation about Extended rather than Core in the autumn term can change an outcome; the same conversation in the spring cannot, because the entry has gone and the ceiling is set.

Then the timetable, which catches Culture Village families out because the district's children attend several different schools. Cambridge allocates every exam centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes a separate timetable per zone. It states plainly that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. Two pupils in the same Jaddaf Waterfront tower at different schools can sit the same paper at different local times, so the only safe document is the one their own school issues.

Results dates differ by series, and this is where a resit decision is genuinely shaped. Pearson's June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026. The November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. So a June grade lands before the new academic year and a November grade lands in the middle of one, which matters for any sixth-form or university conversation that depends on it.

Afterwards comes the window almost nobody uses: enquiries about results, administered by the school's exam office within a board deadline. If a grade looks inconsistent with a student's own marked papers and school evidence, that is the route, and it is short. A family who knows it exists before results day can act in the days when action is possible rather than discovering the option once it has expired.

One correction and one limit. Cambridge's February and March series is offered in India only; UAE candidates sit June and November, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. And IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Culture Village or anywhere else in the UAE: tuition for UAE families is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, while home visiting is a service we operate only in India.

sections.heading: The series counted backwards, and forwards again to results
paragraphs: Here is the administrative year as a single sequence, because this is the part a Culture Village parent is never handed and the part that governs what is possible. The sequence runs: options and provisional tier, entry window, mock examinations, the final eight to twelve weeks, the papers, results, enquiries about results, and then either a done deal or a November entry. Eight stages, each with a different available action.

The stages are not equally forgiving. Before the entry window, almost everything is changeable: subject list, tier, even board in some schools. After it, the ceiling is fixed and the work becomes maximising within it. Before results, the work is preparation; after results, the only remaining levers are a remark enquiry and a retake entry, both of which run to short deadlines through the school rather than the family.

The stage families most often misread is the mock, because schools describe it as practice to students while using it as evidence. Mock results feed tier confirmation where an entry has not closed, setting and grouping decisions, and identification of who needs intervention. A student approaching the mock casually is supplying the school with a worse sample of their ability than necessary, at exactly the moment when decisions are being taken on it.

Where dates below are given, they are published and backward-looking so that they can be checked. Where the date is school-set or board-set for a future series, the table names the month or says who sets it, because boards revise published windows and Pearson explicitly publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series. The right habit is to work from the live official timetable and the school's issued copy.

sections.heading: Zone timetables, and why your child's paper time is not your neighbour's
paragraphs: This is the administrative detail that produces the most avoidable damage and almost nobody in this market mentions it. Cambridge allocates every exam centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes a separate version of the timetable for each. Its own guidance states that it is essential to use the correct version for the centre's zone, and that Cambridge cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used.

For a district like Culture Village, where no school sits inside the community and pupils are spread across several clusters, this has a direct consequence. Two Year 11 students living in the same Jaddaf Waterfront building, one at a school in Al Jaddaf and one at a school in Nad Al Sheba, are candidates at different centres. Those centres may sit in different zones, and the same paper may therefore be scheduled at a different local time for each of them.

The practical rule is simple and worth enforcing at home. Print the timetable the school issues, put it somewhere visible, and give the tutor the identical copy. Do not work from a version found through a general search, and do not accept a revision plan built from a timetable whose provenance nobody can state. A plan that has the paper order wrong will have the final fortnight's priorities wrong too, which is the quiet cost of this error even when nobody misses an exam.

Pearson's position differs: it publishes one international timetable per series, provisionally first and then finally, and it also publishes provisional timetables for future series. That makes a Pearson plan slightly simpler to build and introduces a different hazard, which is a provisional date treated as settled. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and the correct habit for any future series is to link the live official document rather than restate a date that may be revised.

sections.heading: Results, remarks and the decision rule
paragraphs: Results arrive on known dates and the decision that follows should be written down beforehand. Pearson's published pattern makes the shape clear: June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. A June grade therefore lands before the new academic year and a November grade lands in the middle of one, which changes what the grade can still be used for.

The rule to agree in the spring is one line per subject: what result would trigger a retake and what result would not, measured against the destination the student has actually accepted rather than against a general wish for a higher number. That turns results morning into an action, lets an autumn block be booked while slots still exist, and prevents the common error of retaking a grade that was already sufficient.

The option most families never consider is an enquiry about results. Boards run a window for remarks and reviews, administered through the school's exam office rather than directly by a family, and the deadline is short. If a grade looks inconsistent with the student's own marked work and the school's internal evidence, that is the route to raise it. Knowing the window exists before results day is the difference between acting and discovering the option afterwards.

One honest limit on what a tutoring provider can do here. We cannot submit an enquiry, should not offer to, and have no standing in the process at all. What we can do is help a parent read the evidence: whether the marked internal work and the mock paper performance are consistent with the grade awarded. That is a short conversation and it belongs in the days after results, which is also why we hold some availability in that period rather than booking it out in advance.

sections.heading: When tutors are actually free, and when they are not
paragraphs: No page in this market publishes its own availability, which is strange, because it is the single most useful thing a family planning around a calendar could know. Tutor supply in Dubai is not constant across the year. It is wide when nobody is looking and narrow when everybody is, and the pattern is entirely predictable because every school cohort moves through the year together.

The widest window is the autumn of Year 10 and the early autumn of Year 11. Demand has not concentrated, specialists have capacity, and a family can be genuinely choosy about subject, level and slot. That is also the window in which the cheapest and most effective work happens, because fluency gaps are still narrow and the tier conversation is still live. The two facts reinforce each other and almost nobody acts on either.

The narrowest windows are mock season and the final eight to twelve weeks before a series, in both the June and November cycles. Every cohort in Dubai arrives at the same point within the same fortnight, so demand for a Mathematics or Chemistry specialist peaks simultaneously. In those weeks a family searching for the first time is choosing from whoever remains, which is a different purchase from the one available three months earlier at the same price.

There is one more window worth naming: the fortnight after results. Demand spikes briefly as families digest grades and consider retakes, and it is also the moment when a short conversation about evidence is most valuable. We deliberately keep some capacity there rather than selling it in advance, because a family that needs twenty minutes of honest reading of a result set should not have to wait three weeks for it.

sections.heading: The tier conversation, and the only window it works in
paragraphs: Tier is the most consequential item on the administrative calendar and it is settled quietly. Cambridge Core and Pearson Foundation both carry a grade ceiling that performance cannot exceed. Extended and Higher carry the full range with harder content. Schools decide on Year 10 evidence, indicate provisionally, and then enter candidates within the board's window, after which the ceiling is fixed for that series.

The window in which tutoring changes the decision is therefore narrow: between the provisional indication and the final entry. Inside it, focused work on the specific Extended or Higher topics the department doubts can move the call, because the department is watching particular evidence rather than general effort. Outside it, nothing a tutor does affects the tier, and support becomes about maximising performance within a ceiling somebody else set.

So the question to ask the department is not whether they will reconsider. It is what evidence would change their mind. If the answer names specific topics, that is a short block of targeted work with a measurable outcome. If the answer names general confidence or consistency, the problem is slower and more expensive, and knowing that in Year 10 rather than in Year 11 is worth more than any number of hours bought later.

The consequence of accepting a ceiling is worth stating because it arrives two years later. A Level Mathematics, Physics and Economics, and IB Higher Level sciences, assume the Extended or Higher tier content. A ceiling taken at sixteen for safety can close one of those routes, and reopening it means buying bridging support at post-16 rates, which are higher than IGCSE rates across every band of this market. That is a trade worth making deliberately rather than by default.

sections.heading: Home tutoring in Culture Village, priced and timed
paragraphs: Home tuition is a real option here and the published prices allow a comparison. In-home one-to-one rates in Dubai run from AED 180 to AED 350 on Bestimate's table and from AED 200 to AED 500 from home-tutor providers, with monthly in-home packages of AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 for four two-hour sessions appearing in the market. A qualified subject tutor online is quoted at roughly AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors listing IGCSE from AED 150, and AED 799 a month for eight online sessions circulating. Each figure belongs to the provider named and was read in October 2026.

IB Gram does not send tutors to homes in Culture Village or anywhere else in the UAE. Tuition for UAE families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time, and home visiting is a service we operate only in India. That is stated before the argument rather than after it, so a reader knows whose account of the comparison they are reading.

The timing argument is the one specific to this page. The administrative calendar concentrates demand into the same fortnights across the whole market, and in those fortnights a tutor bounded by driving distance from Jaddaf Waterfront is least likely to have a slot and hardest to replace. A match that can be made or changed inside a week requires a pool that is not geographic, and the week it matters is mock week or the week a resit entry is made.

A second practical point. A full timed paper needs an uninterrupted stretch under proper conditions, and a visiting tutor charging by the hour with a next appointment to reach cannot easily supervise one. In practice the paper gets sat unsupervised, which is adequate for content and useless for timing discipline, which is the thing the paper was meant to measure. A weekend online session can run it properly because nobody is travelling to or from it.

sections.heading: Permits, materials and the claims to check
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, described on u.ae as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. An inspection rating is a judgement about a school and does not transfer to any tutor. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, Cambridge or Pearson, and a KHDA Educational Services Permit applies to training institutes with premises and staff, which we are not and do not claim to be.

Tutoring is regulated by permit, and this one a parent can ask about directly. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. The route is MoHRE's own Private Tutor Licensing service, with no fee and a stated two-working-day completion time.

Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published; a figure circulating in this market could not be verified against any official source, and the ministry was reported as not having specified the amounts or detailed the penalties. So no amount appears here, and any figure quoted to you should be treated as unverified.

On materials, Cambridge and Pearson syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade boundary tables are copyright works. We reference and link them from the boards' own sites rather than reproducing or supplying them as downloads, and in sessions we show the student where the current document lives. Given how much of this page depends on official timetables, that habit matters: a student who can find the live timetable can also check a date a tutor has quoted.

paragraphs: Send four things and the stage of the year you are at: the board, the specification code, the tier, and the series the entry is for, plus two evening windows that genuinely work from Culture Village after the school run. Mention a weekend morning if you have one, because full timed papers belong there and the pre-series cycle depends on them. We match a specification specialist and run one free trial lesson in the slot you intend to keep.

What we do with that information depends on the stage. In Year 10 or the autumn of Year 11 we will usually point at the tier conversation first, because it is free and it changes a ceiling. In mock season we will want the mock date and build backwards from it. In the final eight weeks we will want a timed paper before anything else. After results, we will want the marked evidence and the retake rule, if one was agreed.

If no specialist is free in your window we say so, give a realistic wait, and offer the nearest honest alternative rather than placing a general tutor against a specification. Scarcity concentrates in Additional Mathematics 0606, in Pearson Specification B, and in mock season and the final eight to twelve weeks.
